content: 1. The study published in Pediatrics in 1998 examined the impact of introducing solid foods and the type of food on infant growth, providing insights into early dietary influences on development. 2. Marriott et al. (2003) conducted a randomized controlled trial to investigate weaning practices in preterm infants, published in Archives of Disease in Childhood Fetal and Neonatal Edition, highlighting the unique nutritional needs of this population. 3. Perkin et al. (2018) analyzed data from a randomized clinical trial to explore the association between early introduction of solid foods and infant sleep patterns, as reported in JAMA Pediatrics. 4. Perkin et al. (2016) conducted a randomized trial on the introduction of allergenic foods in breastfed infants, published in the New England Journal of Medicine, to assess its impact on allergy prevention. 5. Skjerven et al. (2020) investigated the use of skin emollients and early complementary feeding to prevent atopic dermatitis in infants through a factorial, multicenter, cluster-randomized trial, as detailed in The Lancet. 6. Kreyberg et al. (2019) studied the use of snus and nicotine during pregnancy in Scandinavia and its implications, as published in ERJ Open Research. 7. Rehbinder et al. (2018) examined whether the amniotic fluid of women with uncomplicated term pregnancies is free of bacteria, as reported in the American Journal of Obstetrics and Gynecology. 8. Sloan et al. (2008) found that early weaning is associated with infant weight and the rate of weight gain, as published in Child: Care, Health & Development. 9. Sreedhara and Banapurmath (2014) studied the nutritional status of infants in relation to complementary feeding practices, as reported in Current Pediatric Research. 10. Sun et al. (2016) investigated the timing of solid food introduction and its impact on infant body mass index, as published in the Journal of Pediatrics. 11. Shim et al. (2011) explored the associations between infant feeding practices and picky eating behaviors in preschool children, as reported in the Journal of the American Dietetic Association. 12. Zhao et al. (2016) identified inappropriate feeding behavior as a significant cause of malnutrition in children aged 6 to 36 months in Myanmar, as published in the American Journal of Tropical Medicine and Hygiene. 13. Miliku et al. (2015) examined the relationship between infant breastfeeding and kidney function in school-aged children, as reported in the American Journal of Kidney Diseases. 14. The WHO Working Group (2002) studied the growth of healthy infants and the timing, type, and frequency of complementary foods, as published in the American Journal of Clinical Nutrition. 15. Hua et al. (2017) investigated the relationship between faecal eosinophil cationic protein, serum immunoglobulin E, and infant feeding practices, as reported in Annals of Clinical Biochemistry. 16. Hollis et al. (2016) explored the age at which solid foods are introduced and its association with feeding difficulties in childhood, as reported in the British Journal of Nutrition. 17. Heinig et al. (1993) conducted the DARLING study to examine the intake and growth of breastfed and formula-fed infants in relation to the timing of complementary food introduction, as published in Acta Paediatrica. 18. Vijayalakshmi et al. (2015) studied knowledge and attitudes regarding complementary feeding and its impact on child growth, as reported in the Journal of Evolution of Medical and Dental Sciences. 19. Huh et al. (2011) investigated the timing of solid food introduction and its association with the risk of obesity in preschool-aged children, as published in Pediatrics. 20. Ahmad et al. (2018) examined complementary feeding practices and the nutritional status of children aged 6 to 23 months in Aceh, Indonesia, as reported in Nutrition Research and Practice. 21. Eaton-Evans and Dugdale (1987) studied the effects of feeding and social factors on diarrhea and vomiting in infants, as published in Archives of Disease in Childhood. 22. Barrera et al. (2016) explored the age at which solid foods are introduced and its association with child obesity at 6 years, as reported in Child Obesity. 23. Bielemann et al. (2018) investigated early feeding practices and the consumption of ultra-processed foods at 6 years of age, as reported in Nutrition. 24. Bell et al. (2018) found that the duration of breastfeeding, but not the timing of solid food introduction, reduces the risk of overweight and obesity in children aged 24 to 36 months, as reported in the International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health. 25. Carneiro et al. (2015) studied the growth of infants attending nursing appointments in childcare, as reported in Revista Gaúcha de Enfermagem. 26. Abraham et al. (2012) examined infant feeding in relation to eating patterns in the second year of life and weight status in the fourth year, as reported in Public Health Nutrition. 27. Asfaw et al. (2015) investigated the prevalence of undernutrition and associated factors among children aged 6 to 59 months in South Ethiopia, as reported in BMC Public Health. 28. Baker et al. (2004) studied the associations between maternal pre-pregnant BMI, breastfeeding duration, and timing of complementary food introduction with infant weight gain, as reported in the American Journal of Clinical Nutrition. 29. Caleyachetty et al. (2013) examined breastfeeding duration, age of starting solids, and high BMI risk in Indian children, as reported in Maternal and Child Nutrition. 30. Davies-Adetugbo and Adetugbo (1997) studied the effect of early complementary feeding on the nutritional status of term infants in rural Nigeria, as reported in Nutrition and Health. 31. Grote et al. (2011) analyzed the introduction of solid food and growth in the first 2 years of life in formula-fed children, as reported in the American Journal of Clinical Nutrition. 32. Joseph et al. (2011) investigated early complementary feeding and the risk of food sensitization in a birth cohort, as reported in the Journal of Allergy and Clinical Immunology. 33. Johnson et al. (2014) explored associations between infant feeding and the size, tempo, and velocity of infant weight gain, as reported in the International Journal of Obesity. 34. de Barse et al. (2012) studied infant feeding and child fussy eating in the Generation R Study, as reported in Appetite. 35. Durmuş et al. (2012) examined infant diet and subcutaneous fat mass in early childhood, as reported in the European Journal of Clinical Nutrition. 36. Kalanda et al. (2006) investigated breastfeeding and complementary feeding practices in relation to morbidity and growth in Malawian infants, as reported in the European Journal of Clinical Nutrition. 37. Leary et al. (2015) studied behavioral early-life exposures and body composition at age 15 years, as reported in Nutrition & Diabetes. 38. Rossiter and Evers (2013) examined infant feeding practices and children's weight status, as reported in the Canadian Journal of Dietetic Practice and Research. 39. Koplin et al. (2010) investigated whether early introduction of egg can prevent egg allergy in infants, as reported in the Journal of Allergy and Clinical Immunology. 40. Mäkelä et al. (2014) studied the impact of maternal overweight on infant feeding patterns, as reported in the European Journal of Clinical Nutrition. 41. Lee et al. (2020) examined the influence of age at complementary food introduction on the development of asthma and atopic dermatitis in Korean children aged 1 to 3 years, as reported in Clinical and Experimental Pediatrics. 42. Luccioli et al. (2014) investigated infant feeding practices and reported food allergies at 6 years of age, as reported in Pediatrics. 43. Lin et al. (2013) studied the timing of solid food introduction and obesity in Hong Kong's Children of 1997 birth cohort, as reported in Pediatrics. 44. Mannan (2018) examined early infant feeding of formula or solid foods and the risk of childhood overweight or obesity in a socioeconomically disadvantaged region of Australia, as reported in the International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health. 45. Murcia et al. (2019) investigated infant feeding practices and sleep development in preschoolers from the EDEN mother-child cohort, as reported in the Journal of Sleep Research. 46. Messayke et al. (2021) studied infant feeding practices and sleep at 1 year of age in the nationwide ELFE cohort, as reported in Maternal & Child Nutrition. 47. Metwally et al. (2016) examined early life predictors of socio-emotional development in a sample of Egyptian infants, as reported in PLoS ONE. 48. Nagahori et al. (2017) investigated malnutrition among vaccinated children aged 0-5 years in Batouri, Republic of Cameroon, as reported in the Journal of General and Family Medicine. 49. Onayade et al. (2004) studied the first six months of growth and illness in exclusively and non-exclusively breastfed infants in Nigeria, as reported in the East African Medical Journal. 50. Orlandi et al. (2017) examined breastfeeding and complementary feeding associated with body composition in 18-19-year-old adolescents in the 1993 Pelotas Birth Cohort, as reported in BMC Nutrition. 51. Owais et al. (2016) investigated the minimum acceptable diet at 9 months and its predictive value for infant growth in rural Bangladesh, as reported in PLoS ONE. 52. Padmadas et al. (2002) studied weaning initiation patterns and subsequent linear growth progression among children aged 2-4 years in India, as reported in the International Journal of Epidemiology. 53. Papoutsou et al. (2018) examined the timing of solid food introduction and its association with later childhood overweight and obesity in the IDEFICS study, as reported in Maternal and Child Nutrition. 54. Davies et al. (1977) studied the effects of solid foods on the growth of bottle-fed infants in the first three months of life, as reported in the British Medical Journal. 55. Rodríguez-Cano et al. (2021) investigated complementary feeding practices and their association with adiposity indicators at 12 months of age, as reported in the Journal of Developmental Origins of Health and Disease. 56. Crume et al. (2014) examined the timing of complementary food introduction and the age at diagnosis of type 1 diabetes in the SEARCH Nutrition Ancillary Study, as reported in the European Journal of Clinical Nutrition. 57. Noppornlertrong and Tantibhaedhyangkul (2016) compared growth, infections, and feeding habits among formula-fed infants starting complementary feeding at 4 to 6 months old with those starting at 6 months old, as reported in the Southeast Asian Journal of Tropical Medicine and Public Health. 58. Meshram et al. (2015) studied the influence of feeding practices and associated factors on the nutritional status of infants in rural areas of Madhya Pradesh, India, as reported in the Asia-Pacific Journal of Public Health. 59. O'Donovan et al. (2016) found that neonatal adiposity increases the risk of atopic dermatitis during the first year of life, as reported in the Journal of Allergy and Clinical Immunology. 60. Morgen et al. (2018) examined breastfeeding and complementary feeding in relation to BMI and overweight at ages 7 and 11 years, as reported in the American Journal of Clinical Nutrition. 61. Quigley et al. (2009) studied infant feeding, solid foods, and hospitalization in the first 8 months after birth, as reported in Archives of Disease in Childhood. 62. Moss and Yeaton (2014) investigated the potentially protective benefits of breastfeeding and delaying solid foods on early childhood healthy and obese weight status, as reported in the Maternal & Child Health Journal. 63. Vehapoglu et al. (2014) examined early infant feeding practices and their relation to childhood obesity, as reported in the Journal of Pediatric Endocrinology and Metabolism. 64. Veena et al. (2010) studied infant feeding practices and childhood cognitive performance in South India, as reported in Archives of Disease in Childhood. 65. van den Hooven et al. (2016) investigated associations of breastfeeding patterns and the introduction of solid foods with childhood bone mass, as reported in the British Journal of Nutrition. 66. Vafa et al. (2012) examined the relationship between breastfeeding and obesity in childhood, as reported in the Journal of Health, Population, and Nutrition.
